item.title: Public Tour of Duke Chapel — Sun Oct 4, 12:15 PM — Duke Chapel
item.description:
Learn about the history, architecture, and life of Duke Chapel on this tour, which is free and open to the public.
The tour begins at 12:15 p.m., or immediately following the conclusion of the Sunday morning service, and lasts approximately forty-five minutes. No reservation is required, but if you plan to bring a large group, please notify us in advance. Meet the docent on the front steps of the Chapel.
Paid parking is available on a first-come, first-served basis in the Bryan Center Parking Lot at 125 Science Drive. ADA parking is available in the Bryan Center Surface Lot at the same address.
Source: Duke University

item.title: Blessing of the Animals — Sun Oct 4, 3:00 PM — Duke Chapel Quad
item.description:
Dogs, cats, and other animals will join ministers and the Durham Children's Choir for this Blessing of the Animals worship service on the Duke Chapel Quad. Pet owners are welcome to bring their animals to receive a blessing as part of the service. The service will last about thirty minutes and includes music from the choir, scripture readings, and a sermon. Individual animal blessings will take place immediately after the service.
*** Those bringing pets are responsible for their animals and are asked to bring only pets that will be safe around children and other animals. ***
The Blessing of the Animals service is inspired by St. Francis of Assisi, a thirteenth-century Italian friar who lived a life of voluntary poverty and is known for his love of animals. He believed the natural world could give glory to God, writing in his song Canticle of the Sun, "Be praised, my Lord, through all your creatures."
Source: Duke University

item.title: NCJSS Welcomes Ayelet Brinn — Sun Oct 4, 3:00 PM — John Hope Franklin Center 230-232
item.description:
The North Carolina Jewish Studies Seminar welcomes Ayelet Brinn, Assistant Professor at Hebrew Union College's Skirball (Los Angeles) Campus. Her research focuses on American Jewish history, gender, Yiddish studies, and popular culture.
Brinn holds a PhD in history from the University of Pennsylvania and master's degrees in history and library science from Indiana University. She was previously assistant professor of modern Jewish history and associate director of the Greenberg Center for Judaic Studies at the University of Hartford and has held fellowships at the Hadassah-Brandeis Institute, the Katz Center for Advanced Judaic Studies at the University of Pennsylvania, and at Fordham University and Columbia University.
Her first book, A Revolution in Type: Gender and the Making of the American Yiddish Press, was published by New York University Press in November 2023 and received the the Association for Jewish Studies' 2025 Jordan Schnitzer Award in Modern Jewish History & Cultu

item.title: Choral Evensong Worship Service — Sun Oct 4, 4:00 PM — Duke Chapel
item.description:
For centuries, the church has marked the transition from daytime to evening with psalms, prayer, and song. Duke Chapel's Choral Evensong follows this historic pattern, using the liturgy of the Book of Common Prayer and featuring choral and organ music from the English cathedral tradition, led by the Chapel's Evensong Singers.
Parking is available on a first-come-first-served basis in the Bryan Center garage at 125 Science Drive. ADA parking is available in the Bryan Center Surface Lot at the same address.
The service is livestreamed on the Duke Chapel YouTube channel and broadcast live on channel 12 of the Duke Hospital TV system.
Source: Duke Arts, Duke University

item.title: Durham Square Dance — Sun Oct 4, 5:00 PM — The Pinhook
item.description:
The Durham Square Dance is a community-driven group that supports artistic expression via old time music and collective movement. New and experienced dancers are welcome. You don’t need to bring a partner. There’s a caller who teaches every move and guides you through the wild adventure. A live band plays rippin’ tunes to drive the energy. All in all, your face should hurt by the end from smiling. Family Square Dance, 5-6pm. Slower-paced, for kiddos and their adults. Big Square Dance, 7-9pm. Faster-paced, for anyone out for an adventure. Expect some easy moves, some silly moves, and a good time for anyone. Calling by Nancy Mamlin for both dances. You can choose to pay for a $10, $15, or $20 ticket based on your personal financial situation and ability to support the local arts scene. Kids under 12 are free! One ticket will get you into both dances.
Source: Downtown Durham Inc

item.title: Duke Arts Presents: Camerata Nordica — Sun Oct 4, 7:00 PM — Baldwin Auditorium
item.description:
From one of Europe's premier chamber orchestras comes a group of eight string players for an almost theatrical approach to chamber playing. Standing in a semi-circle, the self-conducted Camerata Nordica octet is "in a class by itself in the way these players so perfectly negotiate the very intricate, most fiercely quick and complex sections" (ClassicsToday.com).
Genius, youth, and a hint of irreverence - these are qualities shared by Mozart, Mendelssohn, and Shostakovich who wrote astonishingly good works at a young age. A standout from Sweden's chamber scene, Camerata Nordica brings them together, opening with a jocular romp by Mozart, while Mendelssohn's Octet serves as the anchor of the concert. Written by the composer at just 16, the frolicsome, high-energy Octet, spins dizzying interplay between eight independent voices. item.title: Library Toolbox for Responsible Research in the Arts & Humanities (Online) — Mon Oct 5, 10:00 AM — None
item.description:
Led by staff from Duke University Libraries, this online Responsible Conduct of Research session for new graduate students serves as an introduction to library resources as well as an overview of essential practices and topics in ethical, responsible research in the arts & humanities. Topics include:
• using library databases and finding materials, • special collections and rare book/manuscript research, • copyright and author's rights, • citation and attribution, • practices in the digital humanities, • research impact and metrics, • research data management, • scholarly networks and communities.
This workshop has been approved for two hours of RCR credit and is intended for new graduate students in the arts & humanities.
Zoom information will be sent via email to registered attendees the day before the session.

item.title: CEE Seminar - Adaptability through control in robotic and active systems — Mon Oct 5, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
One of the hallmarks of adaptive matter is the ability to sense and respond to the environment. How can we engineer soft matter systems to exhibit such behavior? In this talk, I will present our recent findings on systems driven by centimeter-scale actuators (electric motors) and nanometer-scale actuators (myosin motors), using methods from control theory to either design function or probe system properties. Such control-theoretical approaches are often exploited in engineering applications. I will instead emphasize how control in active and robotic systems can help physicists better understand information processing, orchestration of function, and adaptability in living systems.
Source: Duke University

Has the Democratic Party learned the lessons of its 2024 defeats, in terms of not just the contests this November but the future in general? How can Democrats escape Republicans' caricatures of them and promote ideas that transcend partisanship and unite diverse people?
Please join Frank Bruni for a probing conversation - part of his "Independent Thinkers" series of events - with U.S. Representative Jake Auchincloss, a rising Democratic star and one of his party's least predictable and most thoughtful leaders.
Auchincloss, 38, is in his third term in Congress, representing the 4th Congressional District in Massachusetts. He's the inaugural chair of Majority Democrats, a group of lawmakers insistent that the party devote less energy to deriding President Trump and more to developing an agenda that reaches beyond its base. item.title: Duke Arts Create: Ofrenda Screen Printing — Mon Oct 5, 6:00 PM — Arts Annex
item.description:
This event is part of a series of workshops associated with the Día de los Muertos Ofrenda, installed at Duke Chapel from October 2 - November 5. Visitors can make contributions to this altar at any time.
This two-hour workshop will cover the basics of putting images on screens (making a stencil), ink mixing, and how to effectively use a squeegee to get ink through the screen and print multiple copies of an image. The focus is on printing on paper (which is essentially the same process as printing on t-shirts). Everyone will get many chances to print, and you'll have a deluxe, one-of-a-kind, two-color poster to take home! This course is a prerequisite for using the space; after the workshop everyone who attends the class will be on the "approved printers" list and can use the Duke Arts Annex Print Studio at will.

item.description:

In this session, learn the basics of floral design from retired floral designer Patty Stimmel, who worked in Washington, D.C. as a designer for the British Embassy, the White House and Hillwood Museum and Gardens. Patty will demonstrate how to prepare a container for designing a floral centerpiece, as well as the proper way to condition flowers and foliage for longevity. This series of free demonstrations and workshops will take place in the Pelham-Cullen Classroom inside the Barnes Welcome Center. No registration required. Seating is limited and available on a first-come, first-served basis. Doors open 15 min before scheduled start time.

item.description:
The AIHC—with support from its community partners, the North Carolina Commission of Indian Affairs and the North Carolina American Indian Commission—has been the culminating event in honor of American Indian Heritage Month in North Carolina for three decades.
The celebration highlights traditional and contemporary artistic, historical, and cultural contributions of American Indian communities in North Carolina. item.description: NC State LIVE and the Gregg Museum of Art & Design have partnered to present Well-Being Concerts, featuring a family with rich connections to the university and the museum. The late architect Phil Freelon, an NC State College of Design alumnus, led the team that designed the Gregg’s new home, which opened in 2017. Phil Freelon's widow and son, Nnenna and Pierce Freelon, are a Grammy-nominated mother-son musical duo known for their collaborative children’s album, AnceStars. Nnenna Freelon is an acclaimed composer, podcaster, author and advocate for arts education. In addition to his music career, Pierce Freelon is a picture book author, podcaster and ice cream maker. The duo will perform at the Gregg inside the gallery featuring the exhibition Grounded by artist-in-residence Maya Freelon, Phil and Nnenna Freelon’s daughter. item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Thu Dec 31, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: You Are Here Exhibition — Thu Dec 31, 10:00 AM — Witherspoon Student Center
item.description:
Join the African American Cultural Center to experience ariana Farquharson's You Are Here: Geolocating the Self through the Familiar in the Midst of the Unfamiliar. The exhibition is a speculative, immersive world-building study that invites guests to explore (geo)locating self and home amid a rapidly and frequently changing post-pandemic “new” world. It will be on display in the art gallery at the African American Cultural Center from Oct. 28, 2026, to Feb. 28, 2027. A behind-the-scenes look at the exhibition is set for Nov. 11.
Source: NC State African American Cultural Center
